1.pericope_label: Whatsoever man killeth an ox, and bringeth it not unto the door of the tabernacle

schools.summary: Show first why the chapter stands where it does. The Day of Atonement had just purged the whole community from all their sins and presented them a holy nation before the Lord once a year; hence it is now followed by regulations concerning every-day life, the observance of which is to foster the holiness secured on that particular day. Take the four chapters that follow as one block under the heading that Israel is not to walk in the way of the heathen and of the Canaanites but in the ordinances of Jehovah, since all the commandments in them relate to holiness of life; and treat this one as holiness of food, which places the eating of food on the part of the Israelites in the closest relation to their calling as the holy nation of Jehovah. Then draw attention to a phrase that is easily read past. The words unto all the children of Israel are here used for the first time. Hitherto the divine communications were made in seven distinguishable ways: to Moses alone; to Moses with the command to speak to Aaron; to Moses with the command to speak to Aaron and his sons; to Moses with a command to speak to the children of Israel; to Moses and Aaron conjointly, without being ordered to speak to the people; to Moses and Aaron conjointly, who are ordered to speak to them; and to Aaron alone. Here the communication is made to Moses alone, and he is commanded to impart it not only to the priesthood but to all the children of Israel at the same time, so that the pontiff and the priests are put on a level with the ordinary Israelite as far as this regulation is concerned. Note that the phrase recurs only twice more in the book, and that the added formula about what the Lord has commanded is used to mark the importance of the law that follows. On the law itself, hold that it refers to the three kinds of sacrificial quadruped when they are intended for private use, and prove it from the vocabulary, since the text says killeth and not sacrificeth, and from comparing the third and fourth verses with the eighth and ninth. Render the clause about the door better as the entrance of the tent of meeting, and state the penalty exactly: if a man does not bring the animal to the place where the sacrifices are killed and offer it first as a peace offering, he is to be regarded as wantonly shedding blood, and such slaughtering is reckoned as blood-guiltiness and punished with extermination. Then give the reason assigned in the fifth to seventh verses, that the Israelites may bring their slain-offerings before the door as peace-offerings, and no more offer their sacrifices to the field-devils after whom they go a whoring.

Keep the exposition close to the persons addressed and to what they would have understood. Note that the word came to Moses after the law of the day of atonement had been given, and that Aaron and his sons are named because they were now constituted priests, the business of whose office it was to offer the sacrifices of the people, ordinary and extraordinary. Take the opening clause about the man of the house of Israel to include every rank without exception, whether high or low, rich or poor. On the requirement itself, observe that near the door of the tabernacle stood the altar of burnt offering and the priests ready for such service, and that the Lord would have every sacrifice brought thither. Explain what the practice had been before: until the tabernacle was erected the people were used to offer in the open field, and it was lawful for them then to do so, and on high places; but it is unlawful now, though this was sometimes dispensed with by the Lord and was done by some of his prophets, by Samuel and David and Elijah, though not by priests. On the seventh verse, weigh carefully how far the charge is to be pressed. That they had sacrificed to devils is monstrously shocking, and especially in a people who had the knowledge of the true God; such idolatry has been committed in other parts of the world, as when the inhabitants of Hispaniola were found to be worshippers of images in the likeness of painted devils, which they took to be mediators of the one eternal and invisible God, and as is reported of places in the East Indies. But one can hardly think the Israelites would give in to idolatry quite so gross; and therefore by devils may be meant idols in general, since if men do not worship God and Christ, let them worship what they will, it is only worshipping devils. Support that reading from the way the calves of Jeroboam are themselves called devils, and observe that the golden calf which the Israelites had worshipped but lately in the wilderness might go by the same name. On the eighth and ninth verses, note why the offering had to be brought publicly and by the hand of one of the Lord's priests: by that means it might appear both that the offerer did not take upon himself to be a priest, and that he was not offering it to an idol.

Set out the chapter in brief before expounding it: the people are commanded to bring all the cattle they intend to kill to the door of the tabernacle, where they are to be made an offering to the Lord, and those who disobey are to be cut off; the priest is to sprinkle the blood; they are forbidden to offer sacrifices to devils; and the injunction to bring their offerings to the door is then repeated. On the verb killeth, be careful not to make the law wider than it is: this is not spoken of killing for common use, for such beasts might be killed by any person and in any place, but of killing for sacrifice. Then give four reasons why the sacrifice was tied to the tabernacle. It was appointed in opposition to the heathens, who sacrificed in all places; to cut off occasions of idolatry; to prevent the people's usurpation of the priest's office; and to signify that God would accept no sacrifices but through Christ and in the Church, of both of which the tabernacle was a type. Add the qualification that keeps this from becoming a rigid rule, that though men were tied to this law, God was free to dispense with his own law, which he did sometimes to the prophets. On the words about shedding blood, say that the offender shall be punished as a murderer, and give the reason: because he shed that blood which, though not man's blood, was yet precious, being sacred and appropriated to God, and typically the price by which men's lives were ransomed. Explain also why the peace offerings are named rather than others, not exclusively, but because in these the temptation was more common, since they were the most frequent; more powerful, since part of them belonged to the offerer; and more plausible, since their sanctity was of a lower degree, these being only called holy and allowed in part to the people, whereas the others were called most holy and were wholly appropriated to God or to the priests. On the sacrificing unto devils, put the matter exactly: they did so not directly or intentionally, but by construction and consequence, because the devil is the author of idolatry and is eminently served and honoured by it. And on the whoredom, note that idolatry, especially in God's people, is commonly called whoredom, because it is a violation of that covenant by which they were peculiarly betrothed or married to God.

Begin by showing how the matter stood before this statute, for the law cannot be understood without it. It was allowed to all people to build altars and offer sacrifices to God where they pleased; wherever Abraham had a tent he built an altar, and every master of a family was a priest to his own family, as Job was. Then show what came of that liberty, since this is the reason the liberty was taken away. When every man was his own priest and had an altar of his own, by degrees, as they became vain in their imaginations, they invented gods of their own and offered their sacrifices unto demons. The word used signifies rough or hairy goats, because it is probable that in that shape the evil spirits often appeared to them, to invite their sacrifices and to signify their acceptance of them; for the devil, ever since he became a revolter from God and a rebel against him, has set up for a rival with him and coveted to have divine honours paid him, and had the impudence to solicit our blessed Saviour himself to fall down and worship him. Note that the Israelites had learned this in Egypt, and that some of them practised it even after the God of Israel had so gloriously appeared for them. Say why they are described as going a whoring after these demons: because it was such a breach of their covenant with God as adultery is of the marriage covenant, and because they were as strongly addicted to those idolatrous worships, and as hard to be reclaimed from them, as those who have given themselves over to work all uncleanness with greediness; and it is with reference to this that God calls himself a jealous God. Then state how the law settled the matter, and report the stricter opinion fairly. Some think the children of Israel were by this law forbidden, while they were in the wilderness, to kill any beef or mutton or veal or lamb or goat even for their common eating, except at the door of the tabernacle, where the blood and the fat were to be offered to God upon the altar and the flesh returned to the offerer to be eaten as a peace-offering; and the statute is so worded as to favour that opinion, since it speaks generally of killing any ox or lamb or goat. Note that on this view the constitution was altered when they were entering Canaan.

debates.question: How wide does the word killeth reach?

sides.position: To the three sacrificial quadrupeds when intended for private use, as the vocabulary shows, since the text says killeth and not sacrificeth, and as a comparison of the third and fourth verses with the eighth and ninth confirms
Not to killing for common use at all, since such beasts might be killed by any person or in any place, but to killing for sacrifice only
Some hold that while they were in the wilderness the people might not kill so much as a lamb for their own table except at the door, and that the statute is worded so as to favour that view

debates.question: Why was the rule afterwards relaxed?

sides.position: While they were encamped the thing could be enforced, but once settled in the promised land the distance made it impossible, so they were permitted to pour out the blood at their own dwellings and cover it with dust
On the stricter reading the constitution was altered when they were entering Canaan
Though men were tied to this law, God was free to dispense with his own law, as he did to the prophets

debates.question: What is meant by sacrificing unto devils?

sides.position: The word denotes hairy or shaggy goats, and so goat-like deities; the cult is traceable to the goat-image worshipped at Thmuis, and from that stock come Pan and Silenus, the satyrs and fauns, and the horned and cloven-footed devil of medieval Christianity
The goat shape was the form in which the evil spirits appeared, to invite the sacrifices and to signify their acceptance of them
One can hardly think Israel would descend to idolatry quite so gross; devils may rather mean idols in general, since the calves of Jeroboam are themselves so called
They did it not directly or intentionally but by construction and consequence, the devil being the author of idolatry and eminently served by it

debates.question: Is the going a whoring literal or figurative?

sides.position: Not merely figurative: public prostitution formed a real part of the worship of such deities among the Egyptians, Moabites, Canaanites, Greeks and Romans
Figurative: it was such a breach of covenant with God as adultery is of the marriage covenant, and it is with reference to this that God calls himself a jealous God

outliers.note: Alone builds an argument out of the address itself, showing that the words unto all the children of Israel occur here for the first time, setting the seven earlier patterns of divine communication against it, and concluding that in this regulation alone the high priest and the priesthood stand on a level with the ordinary Israelite.

Alone hesitates to take the charge of sacrificing to devils at face value, doubting that Israel would descend to idolatry quite so gross, and citing the painted images that Columbus found worshipped in Hispaniola as the sort of thing the word would otherwise imply.

themes: What man soever there be of the house of Israel, that killeth an ox, or lamb, or goat
and bringeth it not unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation
they shall no more offer their sacrifices unto devils, after whom they have gone a whoring

10.pericope_label: Whosoever eateth any manner of blood; the life of the flesh is in the blood

schools.summary: Note first that this prohibition is not new: it has already been mentioned twice in this book, and in both instances joined to the prohibition of fat. Explain why it is enacted separately here, namely because of its great importance, and because it follows naturally on the order that the blood of all animals sacrificed in the sanctuary is to be offered to the Lord upon the altar. Add, for exactness, that according to the canons which obtained during the second Temple the blood of clean fishes, of locusts and of the permissible creeping things was exempted from this law. On the threat that God will set his face against that soul, gloss it as making him feel the divine anger, and support the gloss from usage: though the phrase occurs only twice more in this book, and only once in connection with legal enactments, it is clear from other passages that the word face denotes anger which shows itself in the countenance, as when a phrase rendered I will appease him is in the original I will appease his face, and as when what the original gives as the face of the Lord is properly rendered the anger of the Lord. On the eleventh verse, correct the rendering before drawing anything from it. The word given as life in the first clause occurs twice more in the same verse and is in both those instances translated soul; it is immaterial which word is chosen, but it is essential that it be rendered uniformly throughout the passage, and by varying it the older version has unnecessarily increased the difficulty of the verse. Then state what the clause asserts: that the blood is the principle of vitality and constitutes the soul of animal life, which is why blood and life are used interchangeably in Scripture, as when the Psalmist asks what profit there is in his blood and means his life. Render the next clause better as, for I have ordained it upon the altar to make atonement for your souls, since it is because the blood is the principle of life that God has ordained it to be offered as an expiation for the offerer's life. And render the last clause better still as, for it is the blood that maketh atonement by means of the soul: the blood of the victim is identical with its life and represents the soul of the animal, so that God has appointed it as a substitute for the sinner's life, and the life of the sacrifice atones for the life of the offerer. Hence the apostolic remark that without shedding of blood there is no remission. On the twelfth verse, say why the stranger is bound too: because he has submitted to the law of the land, and because his eating it would not only infringe a law he has voluntarily adopted but would lessen the horror with which such indulgence was regarded.

Mark what is peculiar in the sanction of this law. God here not only condemns to death whoever shall have polluted himself by eating blood, but declares that He will Himself take vengeance on such a man though he escape from the hands of the judges; He does not merely prescribe to the judges what it is right for them to do, but asserts for Himself the office of inflicting the punishment. Meet the objection that may be raised against the severity, that it is not consistent that the blood of a brute should be compensated for by the death of a man; and answer that this mode of instruction was necessary for a rude people, lest they should speedily lapse into barbarism. Then meet the complaint that no use remained for the blood. Remind them that since it was given for atonement they would be very ungrateful if they were not content with so great a blessing; since it was the price they were to pay for appeasing God, this employment of it was far to be preferred to food, and if they desired to turn into ordinary food the blood which was destined for the altar, Moses indirectly reproves their ingratitude, for when God took away the right of eating it He left them something better. Be exact about how blood atones for souls: it does so in a sacramental manner, since what properly belongs to Christ is transferred to figures and symbols, yet in such a way that the similitude is neither empty nor inefficacious, for in so far as the fathers apprehended Christ in the external sign, atonement was truly exhibited in them. On the strangers, do not understand all such visitors as may have journeyed among them on matters of business, but those who had devoted themselves to the worship of God; for many foreigners, abandoning their superstitions, were circumcised, and it behoved that such as these should be expressly laid under the bonds of the Law, lest they should withdraw themselves from obeying it. Note the corollary, that heathen sojourners were not prohibited from eating blood, since they were allowed to buy for food even flesh that had been torn by beasts. Then explain the apostolic decree by the same principle. Since the patriarchs before the Law had abstained from blood, and its prohibition had no reference to the first table or to the legal service, it came to pass that when the Apostles abrogated the ceremonial law they did not dare to allow the free eating of blood immediately, lest great scandal should arise from this new and unwonted thing. And on the animal life itself, say that it is the principal part which first appears in generation, the fountain of life, the first that lives and the last that dies, the primary seat of the soul, from which motion and pulsation take their rise.

On the threat that God will set his face against the offender, explain both what it means and why it was needed: I will be an enemy to him, and execute vengeance upon him immediately, because such persons would probably do this in private, so that the magistrate could neither know nor punish it. Then let the warning fall as heavily as it is meant to: write that man undone, for ever undone, against whom God sets his face. On the words that the life is in the blood, take them to mean that the life depends upon the blood, and is preserved and nourished by it. Then say in what sense the blood makes atonement, and do not overstate it: it does so typically, and in respect of the blood of Christ which it represented, by which the atonement is really made. From that draw the double reason why the eating was forbidden, since one reason alone does not exhaust the matter. It was forbidden because to eat it was eating up the ransom of their own lives, which in construction was the destroying of themselves; and it was forbidden because it was ingratitude and irreverence towards that sacred blood of Christ which they ought to have had in continual veneration. Then, having given the moral ground, you may add the natural reasons that support it, for they are not to be despised. Blood is highly alkalescent, especially in hot climates, and is therefore subject to speedy putrefaction. It affords a gross nutriment, being very difficult of digestion, so much so that the blood of bulls was used in ancient times as a poison, its extreme viscidity rendering it indigestible by the powers of the human stomach. Where blood was eaten in great quantities, the scurvy was found to be more frequent than at other times. And it appears from history that those nations which lived most upon it were the fiercest and most barbarous, the Scythians, the Tartars, the Arabs of the desert and the Scandinavians among them, some of whom drank the blood of their enemies and made drinking cups of their skulls. Let the hearer see that the revealed reason and the observed one point the same way, and that the law which forbids the eating of blood is not an arbitrary restraint but a mercy.

Observe how much is made of this one prohibition, for that is the first thing the passage teaches. It has been met with twice before in the levitical law, besides the place it had in the precepts given to Noah; and here it is repeated again and again, with reference had to the former laws to this purport, so that a great stress is laid upon it as a law which has more in it than at first view one would think. Note also that it is made binding not only on the house of Israel but on the strangers that sojourned among them, which perhaps was one reason why it was thought advisable, for a time, to forbid blood to the Gentile converts. Then take the penalty and let it be felt: God says he will set his face against that soul that eateth blood, if he do it presumptuously, and will cut him off. God's wrath will be the sinner's ruin; write that man undone, for ever undone, against whom God sets his face, for what creature is able to confront the Creator? Then give the reason annexed, and let it govern the whole. It is the blood that makes atonement for the soul, and it was appointed to make atonement with because the life of the flesh is the blood. The sinner deserved to die, therefore the sacrifice must die; and the blood being so much the life that beasts were ordinarily killed for man's use by the drawing out of all their blood, God appointed the sprinkling or pouring out of the blood of the sacrifice upon the altar to signify that the life of the sacrifice was given to God instead of the sinner's life, and as a ransom or counter-price for it. Therefore without shedding of blood there was no remission. Then apply this in two steps, and keep them apart. In its own time the reason was a very good one, for by this means God would preserve the honour of that way of atonement which he had instituted and keep up in the minds of the people a reverent regard to it; the blood of the covenant being then a sensible object, no blood must be either eaten or trodden under foot as a common thing. But the reason is now superseded, which intimates that the law itself was ceremonial and is no longer in force: the blood of Christ who has come, and we are to look for no other, is that alone which makes atonement for the soul.

debates.question: Why does God reserve the punishment to himself?

sides.position: Because he not only prescribes to the judges what is right for them to do but asserts for himself the office of inflicting the penalty, so that the offender is not safe though he escape the bench
Because such persons would probably do this in private, where the magistrate could neither know nor punish it
The setting of the face denotes anger showing itself in the countenance, as other passages of Scripture use the word

debates.question: How should the life of the flesh is in the blood be rendered?

sides.position: Better the soul of the flesh, since the same word occurs twice more in the verse and is there given as soul; either will do, but it must be rendered uniformly, and the older version has needlessly increased the difficulty by varying it
The life depends upon the blood, and is preserved and nourished by it
It is a claim about animal life that natural philosophy has since confirmed, the vitality of the blood having been revived as a doctrine and established by experiment

debates.question: Who are the strangers that are bound by this law?

sides.position: Not every visitor journeying among them on business, but those who had devoted themselves to the worship of God and been circumcised; heathen sojourners were not under the prohibition, being allowed to buy even flesh torn by beasts
Those who had submitted to the law of the land, whose eating of blood would also lessen the horror with which the Jews regarded it
The binding of the strangers was perhaps one reason why it was thought advisable, for a time, to forbid blood to the Gentile converts
No: the reason given in the text is now superseded, which intimates that the law itself was ceremonial and is no longer in force, since the blood of Christ alone now makes atonement
The Apostles, though they abrogated the ceremonial law, did not dare to allow the free eating of blood at once, lest so new and unwonted a liberty should cause great scandal
The prohibition was enforced by the apostolic decree, as the strangers were bound by it before

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse into a scientific claim and defends it at length, observing that the sentence stood in these writings for thirty-six centuries before philosophy attended to it, and rehearsing an anatomist's experimental proofs of the vitality of the blood, including that blood drawn in extreme cold raises the thermometer as high as blood drawn in heat, and that severing a limb's nerve only paralyses it while severing the artery kills it.

Alone anticipates the complaint that the law leaves no use for the blood, answering that since it was given for atonement they would be ungrateful not to be content, the price of appeasing God being a far better employment of it than food.

themes: whatsoever man there be that eateth any manner of blood; I will even set my face against that soul
For the life of the flesh is in the blood
I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls

13.pericope_label: He shall pour out the blood thereof, and cover it with dust

schools.summary: Mark the extension the law now makes. Hitherto it has mainly discussed the blood of sacrificial animals, or those quadrupeds which were slaughtered at home; in this and the following verses the statute is extended to all other creatures which, though wild, are legally clean and used as food. Then explain why hunters in particular required a rule. Hunting, which was an amusement with other nations of antiquity, was with the serious Hebrew a matter of necessity: it was resorted to in order to exterminate dangerous beasts, but more especially to procure food. Besides the numerous pitfalls, snares and traps so frequently mentioned in Scripture, the Hebrews also employed arms in catching game; and when the animal was wounded, or when the game had to be killed to facilitate its being carried home, the hunters were liable to become careless about the blood. Give the practice that shows the danger was real: the Zabians, when they slew a beast, put the blood into a vessel or into a hole which they dug in the ground, and then sat round and feasted on it; and a case of the hungry army flying upon the spoil, killing the cattle in the field and eating the flesh with the blood, is recorded of Saul's men. It is to prevent such outrages on the sacred blood, which hunters were especially liable to commit when hungry, that the law is here enacted. Note also that during the second Temple the permission was interpreted strictly of the clean wild beasts and fowl, and not of those not permitted to be eaten. On the fourteenth verse, render it so that it actually reasons: as for the soul of all flesh, it is its blood that makes out its soul; that is, this is the case with the soul of all flesh, that its blood makes out its soul. Because the distinguishing characteristic of the blood was that it was the soul of the creature while it lived in the flesh, therefore it was not to be eaten in the case of any animal; and even in the case of animals not proper for sacrifice, it was to be allowed to run out upon the ground and then covered with earth, or, so to speak, buried. Offer the alternative rendering as well, that the life of all flesh is its blood during its life, that is, the life of every creature consists in its blood, but only so long as the blood contains that life, for when it is dried up or coagulated the life has passed away from it. And say plainly that even in those wild animals which, unlike the sacrificial quadrupeds, must never be offered upon the altar, the blood still constitutes the vital principle.

Note first whom the law binds, since the form of speaking used so often in this chapter is there to point it out: the Israelites and the proselytes of righteousness alike. Then take the fifteenth verse and define the offence precisely, for the definition matters. That which died of itself means an animal that died through any disease upon it, or by means of some other creature seizing upon it and worrying it, or that was in any way not lawfully killed. Say how little was needed to break the law: if a man ate ever so little of it, even but the quantity of an olive, it was a breach. Then show why this law is joined to the one before it, since the connection is not accidental. There is a similarity between them, because such creatures must have their blood still in them, not having been regularly let out, and so eating of them would offend against the law just given about blood. Add the observation that carries the matter beyond Israel, for it is worth the hearer's notice how far this statute travelled: it is very probable, as a learned man has thought, that Pythagoras took his notion from this place, and strictly enjoined his followers to abstain from all animals that died of themselves, a rule which the ancient writers who describe his school report of him, and which one of them suggests obtained universally among men. On the sixteenth verse, be exact about what is threatened and about the two distinct failures that incur it. If a man is negligent, and neither washes his clothes nor bathes his flesh, then he shall bear his iniquity, that is, his guilt shall remain upon him and he shall suffer the punishment the law exposes him to, either by the hand of God or by that of the civil magistrate, which is due to persons who enter into the sanctuary in their uncleanness or eat of holy things. And distinguish the penalties as the older Jewish authority distinguishes them: for not washing his body the punishment was cutting off, and for not washing his garments, a beating.

Take the law about the beast that died of itself, or was torn, and give the plain reason for it: because in both cases the blood was retained in the body. Show that this is what governed the later decision of the church, since the council at Jerusalem forbade things strangled as well as blood, because in such beasts the blood was coagulated in the veins and arteries. Then be careful about the state of mind supposed in the offender, for the verse assumes one. He that eateth is he that does so through ignorance or inadvertency; if it was done knowingly, it was more severely punished. Be equally careful about who is meant by the stranger here: it is one who is a proselyte to the Jewish religion, since other strangers were allowed to eat such things, out of which the blood was either not drawn at all or not regularly drawn. On the bearing of iniquity in the last verse, take it to mean the punishment of it, and note what follows for the man himself, that he must therefore offer a sacrifice for it. Then close the chapter with the reflection its subject presses, and do not labour it, for the principal matters have already been handled at length. Everything considered, there is as little propriety in eating blood as there is necessity to do it; and they who will do otherwise must bear their iniquity. If blood eating be no offence, then they have no sin to answer for; but the law has been given, the reason for it has been assigned twice over, and the man who sets it aside does so with his eyes open.

debates.question: Why is a separate rule needed for hunted game?

sides.position: Because the statute is now extended beyond sacrificial animals to wild creatures that are legally clean, and because a hunter who has wounded his game, or must kill it to carry it home, is liable to grow careless about the blood

Because the distinguishing characteristic of the blood is that it was the soul of the creature while it lived, so that even in animals never fit for the altar it must run out on the ground and be covered with earth

debates.question: What is the penalty for neglecting the purification?

sides.position: Cutting off for not washing the body, and a beating for not washing the garments
Excision for entering the sanctuary in a defiled state, and stripes for partaking of the sacrificial meal
The bearing of iniquity means the punishment of it, so that he must offer a sacrifice for it

outliers.note: Alone reconstructs the hunter's situation the law addresses, contrasting hunting as an amusement among other ancient nations with hunting as necessity among the Hebrews, and citing the Zabian practice of catching a slain beast's blood in a vessel or a hole and feasting round it.
Alone follows the statute outside Israel, reporting the suggestion that Pythagoras drew from this very place his strict rule that his followers abstain from all animals which died of themselves.

he shall even pour out the blood thereof, and cover it with dust
every soul that eateth that which died of itself... he shall both wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water
